prompt

PROMPT — one syllable, rhymes with 'stomped'; when something prompts you, it pushes you to act. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To prompt is to cause someone to take an action or to bring about a feeling or response.

The rising prices prompted many families to cut back on spending.

Example

A student watches a documentary about plastic filling the ocean. She can't stop thinking about it all night. The film prompts her to act: the very next morning, she starts a recycling club at her school.

The film moved her to act on her own, without anyone requiring it. Unlike 'force,' which compels someone against their will, to prompt is to nudge or inspire an action.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

trigger: To trigger is to set something off automatically, the way a tripped wire sets off an alarm — once triggered, the reaction simply follows. To prompt is to cause a person to act, leaving room for choice. A smell can trigger a memory on its own; a teacher's question prompts a student to answer.

spur: To spur is to urge someone into faster or harder action, the way a rider's spurs drive a horse — the word carries urgency and pressure. To prompt is milder: it causes an action without any push for speed. Deadlines spur; a polite reminder merely prompts.

motivate: To motivate is to give someone an inner reason or desire to act, and it often works over time — coaches motivate teams through a whole season. To prompt is to cause one specific action in the moment; the prompted person may act at once and then move on, with no lasting drive at all.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

deter: to discourage someone from acting

discourage: to make someone less willing to act

Where it sits · how forcefully the action is pushed — nudge → prompt → compel

nudge vs. prompt: To nudge someone toward an action is weaker than to prompt them — a nudge is the gentlest possible push, while prompting actually sets the action in motion.

compel vs. prompt: To compel is stronger than to prompt: prompting inspires or triggers an action, but compelling forces it to happen whether the person wants to or not.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — pro-

Prefix — pro-: forward, forth (Latin)

Root — mpt

Root — mpt: to take, to bring (from Latin emere, 'to take,' whose past form emptus shows up as -empt- in exempt and preempt; in prompt the e is swallowed)

Put it together

Put it together: Pro- ('forward, forth') + mpt ('to take, to bring' — from Latin emere, whose fuller form -empt- appears in exempt and preempt): Latin promere meant 'to bring forth' — literally to take something forward. When an event prompts you, it brings an action out of you and pushes it forward.

Use the root in a new word: preempt

Use the root in a new word: preempt: The principal preempted the rumor by announcing the schedule change herself first.

Word Building

Word Choice

As a verb, prompt is usually followed by a person or group plus 'to' and an action — 'the news prompted them to act' — describing what causes a response.
